ety.text: From Middle English fade, vad, vade (“faded, pale, withered, weak”), from Middle Dutch vade (“weak, faint, limp”), from Old French fade (“weak, witless”), of obscure origin. Probably from Vulgar Latin *fatidus, from Latin fatuus (“insipid”).
From Middle English fade, fede, of uncertain origin. Compare Old English ġefæd (“orderly, tidy, discreet, well-regulated”). See also fad.

ex:
1825, Francis Jeffrey, Lord Jeffrey, review of Theodric by Thomas Campbell
Passages that are somewhat fade.
His masculine taste gave him a sense of something fade and ludicrous.

senses.d: A golf shot that curves intentionally to the player's right (if they are right-handed) or to the left (if left-handed).
A haircut where the hair is short or shaved on the sides of the head and longer on top. See also high-top fade and low fade.
A gradual decrease in the brightness of a shot or the volume of sound or music (as a means of cutting to a new scene or starting a new song).
The act of disappearing from a place so as not to be found; covert departure.
To hit the ball with the shot called a fade.
ex: The Golden Bear faded the ball from left to right with great consistency, so he seldom had to worry about trouble on the left.

senses.d: To grow weak; to lose strength; to decay; to perish gradually; to wither, as a plant.
ex: The earth mourneth and fadeth away.

senses.d: To lose freshness, color, or brightness; to become faint in hue or tint; hence, to be wanting in color.
To sink away; to disappear gradually; to grow dim; to vanish.
ex: The milkman's whistling faded into the distance.
He makes a swanlike end, / Fading in music.
I tried to get some bets that y'all were fixin' to get married but nobody would fade me.

ety.text: From Vulgar Latin *fatidus, blend of Latin fatuus and vapidus.
Borrowed from Latin īnsulsus (“unsalted”). Doublet of soso.
Inherited from Old French fener, from Vulgar Latin *fenāre, from Latin fenum. Compare Occitan fenar.
From Old French flaistre (“withered”), from Latin flaccidus.
From the adjective biado (alternatively biavo) from Late Latin blāvus, from Old High German blāo (whence also Italian blu via French), cognate with English blue. The s- is an intensifier.

Proto-Indo-European *trísinflu. Proto-Indo-European *d(w)is- Proto-Italic *dis- Latin dis- Old Galician-Portuguese des- Portuguese des- Proto-Indo-European *(s)gʷʰh₂el-der. Proto-Italic *falsō? Classical Latin fallere Vulgar Latin *fallīre Old Galician-Portuguese falirder.
From Old French estioler, modern French étioler (“to make pale”). Compare English etiolate.
From des- + teñir. Compare to English destain.

pt:desbotar.gl: to fade (become faint in hue or tint)

pt:desaparecer.gl: to disappear; to vanish (to become lost, unseen or stop existing)

fr:affadir.gl: to make tasteless, insipid or bland

es:deslucir.gl: to spoil, tarnish, mark, take the shine off

senses.d: That has lost some of its former vividness and colour.
ex: The stop line had a faded appearance but remained visible.

senses.d: That has lost some of its former strength or vigour.
ex: a faded rock star of the 1970s
